content: 1. A dedicated psychosocial support provider should be involved from the beginning of patient care. This individual should be present during the screening process to counsel patients about what to expect inside the wards and, if feasible, should follow the patients daily within the red zone. 2. If it is not possible to have a dedicated psychosocial provider in the red zone, general nurses working in the red zone should be trained and supervised to deliver at least basic psychological support. Basic psychological support guidelines are outlined in the Psychological First Aid during Ebola Virus Disease Outbreaks. 3. Alternatively, a trained psychosocial provider can be stationed in the green zone, close to the red zone, where they can counsel patients across a safe barrier. The ability to communicate in local languages is essential for effective psychosocial support. 4. Providing psychological care while wearing personal protective equipment (PPE) can be physically exhausting for the provider and challenging for the patient, as the inability to see the provider’s face can hinder rapport-building. 5. Support groups for family members and patients post-discharge may be beneficial. If survivors are employed to provide psychosocial support, they require proper training, ongoing mentoring, and psychological support themselves. 6. Terminal patients require skilled and compassionate end-of-life care within the isolation facility. Many Ebola patients remain conscious until the end, while others may experience confusion, agitation, or delirium. Psychosocial and spiritual support for patients and bereavement support for families are critical. 7. Family support at the Ebola Treatment Unit (ETU) should be facilitated where possible. Designate areas for family members to stay outside the facility, create spaces with plexiglass for staff and family to view patients, and encourage stable patients to sit outside to communicate with their families across a fence. 8. Regularly update families about the patient’s condition and inform patients that their families are nearby. Support the use of mobile phones by patients, providing charging facilities or phones if necessary. 9. When safe, allow supervised family visits in full PPE to provide food, encourage oral rehydration solutions (ORS), and interact with children. Clearly explain ETU rules and accompany family members at all times during visits. 10. Child-friendly wards should be designed for constant visual monitoring by staff and family. Younger children require continuous care and support, ideally from family members or survivors. Interaction and physical touch are important for children’s psychological health and to encourage oral fluids and feeding. 11. Wards should include cots, playpens, or beds with grids to prevent children from falling or wandering. Pediatric formulations of medicines, diapers, absorbing pads, and portable toilets should be available to improve care and comfort. As children recover, age-appropriate toys should be provided. 12. Psychological support for health workers and other staff, including survivors assisting the clinical team, is essential to help them cope with high mortality rates, infections among colleagues, and challenging working conditions such as heat stress. 13. Clinical staff face patients with severe pain and discomfort that are difficult to alleviate. They should be prepared to handle these stressful situations. A mental health expert should be part of the medical team to counsel and train staff in psychological skills, communication with patients and families, and stress management. 14. Culturally sensitive counseling support is crucial. Training and supervising local staff to provide psychological support in local languages should be prioritized. During the West Africa Ebola outbreak, there was a high demand for locally trained psychologists, but their availability was limited. 15. Infection prevention and control (IPC) is critical to reducing the spread of infection from patients to health workers, among health workers, and to the community. Transmission primarily occurs through direct contact with blood or body fluids or indirect contact with contaminated environments. 16. Strict adherence to standard precautions, as well as droplet and contact precautions, is necessary for healthcare, environmental, and laboratory workers. Aerosol-generating procedures should be avoided if possible, or adequate protection should be ensured. 17. All healthcare workers, including clinical and non-clinical staff, must use standard precautions when caring for all patients. These include hand hygiene, appropriate PPE, respiratory hygiene, safe waste disposal, and cleaning and disinfection of the environment and patient-care equipment. 18. Hand hygiene should be performed before and after patient contact, after contact with potentially contaminated surfaces, and after removing PPE. Alcohol-based hand rubs are preferred, but soap and water should be used when hands are visibly dirty. 19. Gloves should be changed between patients, and a two-step procedure should be followed to safely disinfect and replace gloves. Double gloves are recommended, and alcohol-based hand rubs are preferred for glove disinfection. 20. Respiratory hygiene should be practiced by all staff, patients, and visitors. This includes covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing, using tissues or masks, and performing hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions. 21. For individuals with respiratory symptoms, source control measures such as wearing a mask and maintaining spatial separation of at least one meter from others should be implemented.
